entries.title: Game-saving defense fires up Cubs in thick of division race: ‘We’re at that point … every game matters’
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>’ defense is so good, replete with Gold Glovers making highlight-reel plays, that you almost have to expect this kind of thing by now, right?</p><p>‘‘I don’t expect it,’’ veteran left-hander <b>Matthew Boyd</b> said, not wanting to anger the baseball gods, ‘‘but it’s amazing.’’</p><p>Boyd’s on-field reaction said a lot more. He screamed with excitement after left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> delivered an on-the-money throw to nail the would-be go-ahead run at the plate in the seventh inning of the Cubs’ 3-2, 10-inning victory Friday against the Pirates.</p><p>And it wasn’t even the only game-saver. Four innings earlier, second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner </b>kept the score tied by making a spectacular stop on a ball ticketed for the outfield. He then immediately threw to third to nab the runner, who had rounded the base too far, ending a scoring chance.</p><p>‘‘Both plays were the difference in the game,’’ manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. ‘‘That’s something we have the ability to do, and it showed up in the biggest moments tonight.’’</p><p>Yes, such plays are commonplace for these Cubs, who statistically have the best defensive squad in the majors.</p><p>But their importance can’t be overstated, especially with the Cubs trying to chase down the National League Central-leading Brewers. They gained a game Friday and sit six games back as the regular season comes down to its final couple of months.</p><p>‘‘I haven’t played in front of a defense this good ever,’’ Boyd said. ‘‘It’s really special when you see the guys flying around and doing stuff like that.</p><p>‘‘We’re at that point. We know what’s ahead of us, and our best baseball is ahead of us. We’re excited about the task that’s in front of us. Every game matters. . . . Wins count the same in April as they do right now, but it’s really exciting to see the opportunity that we have in front of us.’’</p><p>The Cubs were built on a foundation of great defense — see the team Gold Glove they won last season — and it’s the sort of thing that can make the difference, not just in a game in late July but also deep into October.</p><p>‘‘That was just a great example of what we’re capable of on the defensive side of the ball,’’ Happ said. ‘‘There’s a couple of really big plays that saved runs there, but [it’s also] the consistency of the boring plays. . . . [The infielders are] constantly making the routine plays look easy. And they’re not.</p><p>‘‘Just doing that over and over and giving our pitchers the confidence to go and throw strikes and that we’re going to take care of the balls in play? It was a good day.’’</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Chicago fragrance YouTuber stocked luxury cologne collection through mail fraud scheme, investigators say
entries.summary: <p>A 29-year-old Chicago man has been charged with mail fraud and theft after a months-long investigation into fraudulent returns to Nordstrom, officials said.</p><p>After being contacted by Nordstrom in March, the Cook County Sheriff’s Office started looking into luxury fragrances that were returned via mail. But instead of containing the original product, modeling clay was returned in “carefully resealed” boxes, according to a release from the sheriff’s office.</p><p>That kicked off what investigators dubbed, “Operation Eau de Fraud.” An extensive review of records narrowed down the alleged culprit to be Philip Carter, of Portage Park.</p><p>Carter, under his own name, is <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/@phillipcarterxofficial/videos" target="_blank" ><u>a content creator </u></a>on YouTube. Since starting his channel two years ago, he’s uploaded over 100 videos and gained over 3,000 subscribers.</p><p>His content is largely based on in-depth reviews of fragrances. In one video, he says he has over 1,000 fragrances.</p><p>Investigators discovered this YouTube channel, and learned how he may have been stocking his collection, according to the release. Carter, officials said, would order thousands of dollars worth of luxury colognes and fragrances online. Once the items were shipped, he would contact the retailer, like Nordstrom, and request a return.</p><p>But, as was the case in Nordstrom’s experience, the original bottles would be removed from boxes and replaced with modeling clay, or used bottles. Investigators say Carter then resealed the packages and would receive a refund.</p><p>The investigation came to a head Wednesday morning, court records show. The office’s Organized Retail Crime unit searched Carter’s Portage Park apartment and took him into custody, according to the release. It was his 29th birthday.</p><p>Officers recovered 714 fragrances, which are estimated to retail for $250,000, the release said. Ready-to-ship resealed boxes, packages containing modeling clay were found, in addition to a heat gun, glue and packaging materials.</p><p>The next day, the Cook County state’s attorney’s office charged Carter with three counts of mail fraud and three misdemeanor counts of theft by deception.</p><p>Court records indicate that Carter has since been granted pretrial release. Conditions of his release include staying away from Nordstrom and Ulta Beauty locations.</p><p>Carter is scheduled to appear in court on July 29.<br></p>

entries.title: Barack Obama gives WNBA All-Stars wisdom and a little presidential aura
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" target="_blank" >WNBA</a> All-Stars were the first professional players to christen the court at the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>So it was fitting that former President <b>Barack Obama</b>, a devoted basketball fan, surprised the group with a short speech Friday before greeting players individually.</p><p>‘‘The way the game has been going lately, people paying attention to your excellence, it’s been making me happy,’’ Obama said.</p><p>His appearance left an impression on everyone, including on one of the faces of the league.</p><p>Now in her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/07/24/is-caitlin-clark-the-best-point-guard-at-all-star-weekend-relax-shes-definitely-one-of-them" target="_blank" >third season</a>, Fever star <b>Caitlin Clark</b> has helped to bring an enormous new audience to the WNBA. Her massive stardom also has subjected her to scrutiny that often turns ugly and personal.</p><p>Obama called Clark ‘‘fantastic’’ and told her not to let all the ‘‘nonsense’’ get her down. He also acknowledged how difficult it must be to navigate fame at her age.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/24/obama-wnba-all-star-game-changemaker" >Obama drops in at WNBA event inspiring ninth grade girls at presidential center</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>‘‘Sometimes I think people don’t always realize that I’m 24 years old and trying to navigate a lot of different things, trying to play basketball at the same time,’’ Clark said. ‘‘It was cool to hear that from him.’’</p><p>Obama, who said he already had put the court to use in a game of H-O-R-S-E, also reminded Clark not to lose her joy for basketball. She took the message to heart.</p><p>‘‘There are moments that are tiring and exhausting, but I still have the same love and joy for the game that I had when I first got here,’’ Clark said.</p><h3>Copper meets Obama</h3><p>How did former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> star <b>Kahleah Copper</b> feel about meeting Obama?</p><p>‘‘Oh, my God, it was so cool,’’ Copper said. ‘‘The coolest thing for me is just how personable he is. It’s so genuine. He’s like, ‘You’re having a great season. I’m super-proud of you.’ I’m like, ‘You watched me?’ ’’</p><p>Copper, who helped the Sky to the 2021 championship and earned Finals MVP honors, was selected to her sixth All-Star team this season.</p><p>‘‘He’s not general,’’ Copper said of Obama. ‘‘He knows your name, knows how your season is going.’’</p><p>Copper also said it was meaningful for the South Side to have access to a place as impressive as the Obama Center.</p><h3>Delle Donne still has it</h3><p>Retired Sky star <b>Elena Delle Donne</b> hasn’t lost her shooting touch.</p><p>Delle Donne and her teammates dominated the new Shooting Stars competition, which paired current and retired WNBA players with elite high school prospects.</p><p>Representing Team Washington, Delle Donne won alongside Mystics center <b>Shakira Austin</b> and <b>Jezelle Banks</b>, a player from her former high school.</p><p>Delle Donne played for the Sky in 2013-16 and won an MVP with them in 2015.</p><h3>Fudd wins three-point contest</h3><p>Wings rookie <b>Azzi Fudd</b> became the first rookie to win the All-Star three-point contest, scoring 30 points in the finals to top Fire veteran <b>Bridget Carleton</b> (19).</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-010001" name="list-010001"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> Latest on the Sky and WNBA </div> </div> </div> <div class="PageListH-items" data-with-borders data-list-loadmore-items> <div class="PageListH-items-item"><div class="PagePromoB"> <div class="PagePromo-media"><a class="Link" aria-label="Is Caitlin Clark best point guard at All-Star Weekend? entries.title: Trump calls LeBron James 'maybe a racist' compared to Michael Jordan
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said basketball star LeBron James is “maybe a racist” when asked how he stacked up against Hall of Famer Michael Jordan.</p><p>James is the NBA's all-time leading scorer, a four-time champion and a four-time Olympic medalist.</p><p>He has played for the Los Angeles Lakers, Miami Heat and Cleveland Cavaliers. He made headlines July 24 for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nba/2026/07/24/lebron-james-philadelphia-76ers" >signing as a free agent with the Philadelphia 76ers</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nba/2026/07/24/lebron-james-philadelphia-76ers" >LeBron James will close out his career with the Philadelphia 76ers</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Jordan was a six-time champion with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> in the 1990s and a two-time gold medalist at the Olympics. He took off two years at the height of his skills to play baseball.</p><p>Because James and Jordan didn’t play in the same eras, fans debate who is the best player ever.</p><p>Without getting into basketball statistics, Trump put his thumb on the scale for Jordan.</p><p>“Michael Jordan is a guy that’s a friend of mine. Play golf with him. He’s a really good guy,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I think LeBron is — maybe he’s a racist. Maybe he doesn’t like Trump. But I only like people that like me. So I would say Michael Jordan all the way.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/8/4/18418452/president-donald-trump-takes-swipe-at-lebron-james-celebrates-michael-jordan" >Trump and James have a history.</a></p><p>James criticized the president during his first time in a CNN interview with Don Lemon. James said Trump was "using sports to kinda divide us, and that's something that I can't relate to."</p><p>Trump fired back on what was then Twitter that James had made Lemon look smart despite Lemon being what the president called "the dumbest man on television."</p><p><i>Read more at </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com" target="_blank" ><i>usatoday.com</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Struggling Noah Schultz might be odd man out of White Sox' rotation by trade deadline
entries.summary: <p>Rookie left-hander Noah Schultz is scheduled to take his turn in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> rotation next week against the Yankees. Whether he takes the one after that remains to be seen.</p><p>General manager Chris Getz is looking for pitching help, and Schultz’s struggles could make him the odd man out. He’s coming off an outing in which he lasted 3⅔ innings, tying the shortest of his 12 starts this season. With veterans Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde not providing enough length consistently, the Sox can’t afford to have Schultz provide even less.</p><p>The trade deadline Aug. 3 comes one day after Schultz would pitch again. It’s fair to wonder whether he or an acquisition will make that start.</p><p>Schultz might need a reset in Triple-A anyway. Since returning from the injured list July 1, Schultz has allowed 13 earned runs and 24 hits in 18 innings (6.50 ERA). He allowed five runs and 11 hits Tuesday against the Rangers.</p><p>“He’s been working so hard and working on being in the zone, and that is something obviously he was able to do his last start,” manager Will Venable said. “Maybe it came at the cost of a little downtick in some of the stuff. I think his fastball was down maybe a mile an hour on average.</p><p>“You’re just not seeing those swing-and-misses in the zone. While he’s done such a good job to get into the zone, we've got to make sure that we’re getting back to that really crisp stuff and trying to get it in the zone. He’s got a lot to work on, but I think he’s taking steps forward.”</p><p>One of those steps is reducing his walks. After walking seven in 9⅓ innings in his first two starts back from a knee injury, Schultz hasn’t walked anyone in his last two starts, spanning 8⅔ innings.</p><p>“We’re working on just staying loose, a lot of drills to keep me loose,” Schultz told the Sun-Times before heading out to throw in the bullpen. “We found I was just too tense when I was coming set. That led to some inconsistencies with delivery. We think that helped.”</p><p>Schultz has pitched out of the stretch since he was 14 because of his long frame, which is now 6-10, 240 pounds.</p><p>“The less moving parts, the better,” he said. “We’ve learned that with the long limbs, the shorter and quicker the delivery can be, the less room for error there is.”</p><p>But there’s still enough error. Schultz has been working to get more chase on his two-strike pitches. He’s capable of racking up the strikeouts, averaging nearly eight per nine innings this season. Venable thinks Schultz can make such adjustments in bullpen sessions.</p><p>“That’s what we’re trying to do here,” Venable said. “We evaluate every time through [the rotation]. What’s our best five to get us through this? He’s working so hard to make these adjustments, has been able to make some. We just gotta put it all together.”</p><p>The Sox are trying to balance developing their young players while making a playoff push. It’s a tough tightrope to walk. They’ve been managing it with Schultz, and he knows it.</p><p>“It’s a great feeling being able to see the guys around me succeeding,” Schultz said. “Guys picking me up, having my back. There’s games every now and then that we lose, but I think in the big picture, we’re still winning games.</p><p>“It’s great to be able to learn from the guys. The rest of the staff’s been throwing so well that during the games, you’ll see things that they [do]. Just pick their brains and pick up things that you don’t really realize right away.”</p><p>But this isn’t exactly a good time for a rookie pitcher to learn on the job.</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Davis Martin can't escape nightmare sixth inning in White Sox' loss to Astros
entries.summary: <p>Davis Martin was practically in cruise control Friday against the Astros, throwing five scoreless innings and taking a five-run lead into the sixth, having escaped his only two innings with multiple baserunners.</p><p>But he couldn’t escape that nightmare inning.</p><p>The Astros sent 14 batters to the plate and scored eight times, the big blows being Christian Walker’s three-run double and Cam Smith’s two-run home run, sending the White Sox to a 9-5 loss.</p><p>“Just couldn’t get any outs,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “They did a good job putting the ball in play.”</p><p>“It’s unacceptable,” Martin said. “The tone-setting in the sixth inning was really bad on my part, which leads to a bigger inning.”</p><p>That it did. After allowing three hits in five innings, Martin allowed singles to slugger Yordan Alvarez, Jose Altuve and LaMonte Wade and plunked Isaac Paredes.</p><p>“For me, Yordan single, you keep him in the yard, that’s great,” Davis said. “Hit by pitch to Paredes is tough. But then I look at it like, Altuve hits that ball a couple feet to the left, Wade a couple feet to the right, it’s a completely different inning. I know it’s all wish in one hand and s–t in the other and see which one fills up first. It’s baseball. Baseball happened. It sucks.”</p><p>Venable went to left-hander Bryan Hudson, who promptly allowed the double and homer. Hudson had closed out the Sox’ 4-2 victory Wednesday against the Rangers.</p><p>“We’re thinking that Huddy against anybody, lefty or righty, is a good person to pick [us] up,” Venable said. “When you give up eight runs in that spot, that’s probably a decision that I made or something that I missed. As far as the timing with Huddy, I think there’s an argument for a batter before there. But Davis is in a good spot. He hadn’t given up a run yet.”</p><p>“Huddy’s our guy, somebody that you trust in every situation. You mentioned him closing last outing. Just one of those where something along the way didn’t drop him in right, and obviously they were able to capitalize and score a bunch of runs.”</p><p>Astros starter Spencer Arrighetti, who allowed three runs in the first, left with nerve irritation in his right foot after throwing a few warmup pitches before the second. The Sox scored only two runs the rest of the way in what became a bullpen game for the Astros.</p><h3>Mune ‘in a good spot’</h3><p>Munetaka Murakami hasn’t homered in a game since May 27, when he hit his third in three days. His 20 homers have been surpassed by Miguel Vargas (21) and Colson Montgomery (24) on the team. But manager Will Venable thinks the slugging first baseman is in a good spot.</p><p>“I think the last couple games, [we] saw him get that leg up and get ready a lot earlier,” Venable said. “To me, that’s a good sign that he’s putting himself in a much better position, that the timing is getting closer and closer.</p><p>“We see him putting more and more balls in play. Hasn’t clicked that one yet, but he continues to put himself in a good spot. And along the way, he continues to make really good swing decisions and takes, as well.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Sox rookie right fielder Braden Montgomery had his first three-hit game, singling in each of his first three at-bats. Two of them were with two strikes. He finished 3-for-5 with a run and an RBI.</p><p>• Caleb Bonemer, the Sox’ top-ranked prospect, left Double-A Birmingham’s game after being hit in the head by a pitch. Preliminary tests indicate he doesn’t have a concussion.</p><p>• Right-hander Jordan Leasure threw in the bullpen as he continues his recovery from a strained right flexor.</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: What's your favorite iconic Chicago sign? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers to tell us their favorite iconic Chicago sign. Here's what they told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Trim and Tidy Cleaners in Jefferson Park. The sign hasn't changed in 50 years."<br><i>— Jon Larson</i></p><p>"My favorite Chicago sign was the Magikist sign along the Kennedy [Expressway]. As a kid, when I saw that sign, I had some idea of how much longer till the family station wagon arrived downtown or arrived home from a trip downtown. ... I always sat in the third row, which faced backwards, and got to stare at the lips for a long time as they filled in with vertical lines of bright, red lights over and over."<br><i>— Loretta Namovic</i></p><p>"The Harold’s Chicken Shack sign. IYKYK."<br><i>— Brian Althimer</i></p><p>"The Chicago Skyway Toll Bridge signs and their infamous typography (see 'The Blues Brothers')."<br><i>— Marty Regan</i></p><p>"The Chicago Theater sign in the evening while watching all the excited people taking in a concert."<br><i>— Terrence Camodeca</i></p><p>"The Ebony/Jet sign, because it meant I was out of southern Indiana."<br>— Scott Singer</p><p>“The lottery sign on I-94 when it still had the rotating panels. As a kid I couldn't wrap my head around how they worked.”<br><i>— Dave Levin</i></p><p>"The Baby Ruth sign that used to be on Lake Shore Drive."<br><i>— Tony Galati</i></p><p>"The Little Palestine Way sign at 87th Street and Harlem Avenue. It's beautiful."<br><i>— Ali Salman</i></p><p>"The [Native American] at 63rd Street and Pulaski Road. It’s a South Side landmark."<br><i>— Lulu Hz</i></p><p>"Old Style signs."<br><i>— Patricia Simmons</i></p><p>"The Town & Country Liquor Mart neon sign in Brighton Park."<br><i>— Jaime Duque</i></p><p>"The giant Rainbow Cone on the original location in Beverly."<br><i>— Bobby Veejay Marley</i></p><p>“The dancing hot dogs on the roof of Superdawg at Milwaukee and Devon avenues.”<br><i>— JoAnne Kempf</i></p><p>"Kiddieland."<br><i>— Angelica Aragón Rooney</i></p><p>"PBR over South Water Street — obvs."<br><i>— Jim Pabst</i></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Widow has second thoughts about rekindled romance
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> After a four-year battle with cancer, my husband of 27 years passed away. After his death, I was contacted by a guy I had been involved with 40 years before. He said he wanted me to know that he was there for me if I needed to talk or just needed some company. I told him how much I appreciated it and I would call if I felt he could help.</p><p>This man was someone I had loved intensely. We had dated for seven years when he broke my heart. He was seeing other people behind my back, and when I found out, I broke up with him. We always managed to stay in touch, though. He would call to wish me happy birthday or just say hi. We remained friends. He dated a couple of people I knew, and we would run into each other a couple of times a year.</p><p>Well, we are now seeing each other again. He has told me how sorry he is for breaking my heart all those years ago. He says he knows that being a man is not being with every woman you possibly can be with but being willing to commit to the one woman you know you love. He says he knows he made a mistake and he loves me and wants us to spend the rest of our lives together.</p><p>The problem: I can't stop thinking about all the women he has been with and how I will never be able to measure up to them. There's nothing special about me. I'm not beautiful, I don't have a "killer body" and I don't have a lot of money. I don't want to ruin what is possibly the best thing that has ever happened to me, but I just can't seem to move past this. What can I do to move forward from his past? — <i>BACK WHERE I STARTED IN TENNESSEE</i></p><p><b>DEAR BACK:</b> The only thing that could ruin what is possibly the best thing that has ever happened to you is your low level of self-esteem. This man appears to have matured in the years since you broke up with him. He isn't after a raving beauty, a woman built like a racing sloop or a sugar mama. He is interested in the person you are.</p><p>Please ask your doctor for a referral to a licensed mental health professional who can help you make a serious attitude adjustment before your insecurity ruins what could potentially be a happy future.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been lucky. I have done well and lived a good life. I'm married (my third time), and I have adult children and grandkids. For most of my life, I have had an active sex life. Much of it I wouldn't want my children to know about while I'm alive, but it could make for some erotic reading years after I'm gone. Should I write my honest accounting covering 50 years and leave it for posterity? — <i>TALES TO TELL IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR TALES:</b> For the sake of your children, their spouses, and your grandchildren please resist the urge to recount in detail your sexual history. When you depart this earthly plane, leave them with at least a few illusions, I'm begging you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To order "How to Write Letters for All Occasions," send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby — Letter Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: How we photographed Lithuanians' passion for democracy
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from photojournalist and Photo Desk Editor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/ashlee-rezin" target="_blank" >Ashlee Rezin</a>. Follow her on <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Ashlee_Rezin" target="_blank" >X</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/ashleerezin/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>About 60,000 Lithuanian Americans live in the Chicago area, and my colleague Stephanie Zimmermann's late mother was one of them. She fled as a child when the Soviet reoccupation began in 1944. When Stephanie first approached me about traveling to Lithuania, to eventually produce six stories, my knee-jerk response was, "Why?" But Stephanie's enthusiasm is infectious, and I soon also fell in love with the small Baltic country with deep roots in Chicago. Lithuania declared independence from the Soviet Union as recently as 1990, and I was impressed by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/07/22/america-250-learn-lithuania-democracy-aided-chicagoans" >the citizenry’s civic engagement</a>. Stephanie and I conducted interviews with more than 50 Lithuanians during the two weeks of our trip, and the majority were ready to work to preserve their country's independence, including as members of the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union. It was a privilege to witness such passion in defense of rights many Americans — including myself — take for granted, such as free speech and freedom of the press.</p><p></p><h3>How I got this photo</h3><p>My last day in Vilnius was spent at a free speech protest in Cathedral Square. Thousands draped Lithuanian flags over their shoulders and stood in the rain for hours. The protest was one of several that have been staged after a right-wing populist party in the government’s ruling coalition tried to control the country’s Ministry of Culture and threatened the independence of its public broadcaster, Lithuanian Radio and Television. The size of the crowd was overwhelming. To show the scale of the protest, I sought high ground up a flight of stairs, behind the stage. From there, I spotted a young girl, chanting and singing as if she herself had survived the Soviet Union's repression at least 36 years ago. I wondered if her parents or grandparents told her stories of 1991's “Bloody Sunday,” when Soviet soldiers killed 14 Lithuanians who were trying to stop the seizure of the Vilnius TV Tower. Regardless, she was clearly brought up with an admirable passion for democracy. </p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" entries.title: Canada wildfire smoke ignites urgency for climate action
entries.summary: <p>Chicagoans are once again <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" >breathing dangerous air </a>from Canadian wildfires, a reminder that the climate crisis is no longer distant. That reality hit me even harder on a recent hike at <a class="Link" href="Denali National Park and Preserve" target="_blank" >Denali National Park and Preserve</a>, where I learned that more than 1 million acres of Alaskan tundra and forest burned last year — roughly double California’s losses and nearly triple those in Oregon and Utah combined.</p><p>Illinois rarely sees wildfires, but our exposure to unhealthy air is becoming routine. Thick smoke drifting in from Canada recently pushed Chicago to the top of the list of the world’s most‑polluted cities for the second summer in a row, according to the global monitoring platform <a class="Link" href="https://www.iqair.com/" target="_blank" >IQAir</a>.</p><p>Every year, our destabilized climate drives more extremes: megafires, floods, droughts and heat waves. That’s why this week, I’ll join 40 other Illinois volunteers — and hundreds more from around the country — in Washington, D.C., for the<a class="Link" href="https://citizensclimatelobby.org/climate-change-conferences/summer/" target="_blank" > Citizens’ Climate Lobby’s Summer Conference and Lobby Day</a>. We’ll meet with members of Congress to encourage bipartisan action to protect forests and reduce the conditions fueling severe heat waves and worsening wildfires.</p><p>Among those traveling with us are Illinois college students who see climate policy not as an abstraction, but as a matter of public health, economic opportunity and generational responsibility.</p><p>Illinois State University senior Kayleigh Anderson says a human rights course reshaped her understanding of climate change: “One concept that stuck with me was that climate change is a ‘threat multiplier.’ It makes existing challenges like poverty, food insecurity, displacement and public health issues even worse. That was when I realized climate change is not just an environmental issue; it’s a human rights issue."</p><p>Southern Illinois University senior Haresh Kittu brings a similar urgency: “A dirtier, more polluted society will only increase the burden for our children to bear. A day may soon come when our children struggle to breathe on the same planet that once gave us life."</p><p>Climate and energy debates often get trapped in partisanship. But America needs a healthy environment, a strong economy and reliable, affordable energy. The right policies can advance all three. That’s why we’re urging Congress to support permitting reform that speeds clean energy build-out while protecting communities and natural resources.</p><p><i>Joe Tedino</i>, <i>Lake View</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fb0000" name="module-fb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>TV president hijacks current episodes of America’s story </h3><p>Neil Steinberg pointed out in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/07/12/ai-artificial-intelligence-radio-technology-new-steinberg" >recent column</a> that radio did not destroy America. True. Instead, it is television that has destroyed America. Television has turned all of us into a nation of passive viewers.</p><p>Take the war in Iran. If the news is too much of a downer, just flip the channel.</p><p>Television created a pathway for TV personalities to enter politics. Look at Donald Trump. Before he came down that <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/jun/13/donald-trump-presidential-campaign-speech-eyewitness-memories" target="_blank" >escalator</a> in 2015, he had zero experience as a politician. None. But he knows how to entertain people.</p><p>People say that he lies, which isn't entirely accurate. Trump is writing his own script. He will promise something, and that something ends up taking place two or three weeks later. Will he do it? Won’t he do it? Stay tuned for the next exciting episode of "Trump the President."</p><p>Trump's view of the world has also been shaped by movies and TV. He says he knows more about combat than our generals and has likely watched more war movies than any other president. He knows exactly how this current episode of "Trump at War" ends. The enemy will be totally destroyed, and he, the victor, will stand triumphant.</p><p>What frustrates Trump so much is that many in the news business keep going off script. They criticize him. They say that he is wrong. Instead of praising him, they are trying to spoil his ratings with facts. </p><p>When Trump isn't happy with the props he's been given at the nation’s capital, he changes the scenery. The Oval Office — too plain. The East Wing — replace it with a magnificent <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/investigations/2026/06/30/trump-ballroom-built-under-secret-500m-no-bid-contract/" target="_blank" >ballroom</a> where he can give speeches and be the center of attention. The district itself needs to be beautified — Trump's planned <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/05/27/democrats-bill-would-block-trump-planned-250-foot-triumphal-arch/" target="_blank" >250-foot triumphal arch</a> will dominate the capital’s skyline and be a constant reminder of his "greatness."</p><p>This TV president's behavior should be a call to action. What our country desperately needs is an amendment to the Constitution that says that anyone running for Congress or the presidency must have at least six years of previous experience as a politician. If such an amendment were added, it would keep the ego freaks and TV personalities out of politics.</p><p><i>William Dodd Brown, Lincoln Square </i></p><h3>Trump ‘made in China’ election fraud allegations</h3><p>During his July 16 <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-primetime-address-elections-5c84a59dffc20c12ed2fcb822fa950c9" target="_blank" >primetime address</a>, President Donald Trump falsely claimed again that our elections, specifically the 2020 election, can't be trusted. This time, he alleged <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2k9wvv5wyo" target="_blank" >Chinese interference</a> in 2020. Over the years, he has also blamed voting by noncitizens, rigged voting machines and election fraud.</p><p>If these allegations were true, Trump would have had the same issues with the 2024 election. At that time, we had a Democratic president and a Democrat-controlled Senate. Yet, not only did Trump win, but the Republicans took control of the Senate and the House. Either the 2024 election was also rigged (which would call into question the legitimacy of Trump's second term) or the problems that our elections had in 2020, including the <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-trumps-address-on-china-the-2020-election-and-what-documents-show" target="_blank" >supposed Chinese interference</a>, were somehow fixed in time for the 2024 election. Of course, all of this is nonsense. It's just another in a long line of instances where Trump has put his own interests — whether it be his ego, finances or vendettas — above those of the country. Anyone who thinks otherwise needs to start considering the facts.</p><p><i>Jeffrey Meyer, Roscoe Village</i></p><h3>AI can help track unclaimed-property dollars</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ILCS/details?ActID=3794&ActName=Revised+Uniform+Unclaimed+Property+Act.&ChapAct=765+ILCS+1026%2F&Chapter=PROPERTY&ChapterID=62+&MajorTopic=RIGHTS+AND+REMEDIES&Print=True&SeqEnd=11300000&SeqStart=200000" target="_blank" >Illinois law</a> requires some excess money from its Unclaimed Property Trust Fund to be transferred to the State Pensions Fund. Beginning July 1, 2027, those deposits are scheduled to be divided among five state retirement systems to reduce their unfunded liabilities.</p><p>The owners can still claim their money later, and Illinois remains obligated to pay valid claims. But the arrangement creates an unavoidable conflict. The state is supposed to find the owners. It also benefits when they remain lost.</p><p>Illinois is holding more than <a class="Link" href="https://illinoistreasurer.gov/home/individuals/unclaimed-property/" target="_blank" >$5 billion</a> in unclaimed property. Treasurer Michael Frerichs deserves credit for improving the state’s I-Cash program. His office says it has returned more than $2.5 billion to over 2.5 million people, businesses and nonprofits since 2015.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoistreasurer.gov/home/individuals/money-match-faq/" target="_blank" >Illinois also operates Enhanced Money Match</a>, which compares unclaimed-property records with information held by other state agencies. When it verifies a straightforward match, the state sends the owner a check automatically.</p><p>Since 2018, the program has returned more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/il-state-treasurer-office-returns-181937533.html" target="_blank" >$130 million</a> to more than 870,000 people.</p><p>That proves Illinois does not have to wait for people to search. It can find them.</p><p>But the program generally covers simple cash claims involving one owner. Joint property, stocks, bonds, business accounts, safe deposit box contents and estate claims often remain outside the automatic system.</p><p>The easy money goes out. Much of the $5 billion stays.</p><p>A conventional search box waits for someone to enter the right name, spelling and state. People miss records under maiden names, initials, old addresses, former employers, business names and deceased relatives. They search once, find nothing and never return.</p><p>Artificial intelligence could reverse that process.</p><p>AI could start with a property record, compare names, addresses, employers, businesses, relatives and reporting companies, then score the strength of a likely match. The state would still verify ownership and approve payments. AI would not touch the money or bypass fraud controls. It would simply help locate people.</p><p>Illinois could build a stronger system than any private company because it has the records and government data, subject to strict legal and privacy limits.</p><p>Frerichs should expand Enhanced Money Match using AI and verified government records, then report each year how much Illinois receives, returns and transfers to pension systems.</p><p>The goal should not be managing a $5 billion pile more efficiently. It should be shrinking it.</p><p>Now that Illinois is using excess unclaimed-property money to fill pension holes, it should use every available tool to find the people whose money is filling them.</p><p><i>Mark Lewyn, founder, </i><a class="Link" href="http://unclaimedmoneyguy.com/" target="_blank" ><i>UnclaimedMoneyGuy.com</i></a></p><h3>Legislation will help children worldwide </h3><p>Our earliest years are often the ones that shape the rest of our lives, and yet millions of children around the world still grow up without the nutrition, healthcare, safety and early stimulation needed to develop safely and fully. Horrible as that is, this is not only a humanitarian concern. This unaddressed cycle of global poverty affects global stability, education standards, world economic growth and the quality of life all children everywhere will inherit.</p><p>Congress has a practical and bipartisan way to help. The proposed <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/6347" target="_blank" >Global Child Thrive Reauthorization Act</a> would continue U.S. support for international early childhood development programs through 2030 and mandate the secretary of state to appoint a special adviser for orphans and vulnerable children. These actions alone will help integrate basic, proven interventions such as nutritional supplementation, childcare support and early learning aid into our country’s existing foreign policy.</p><p>As an intern with <a class="Link" href="https://borgenproject.org/" target="_blank" >the Borgen Project</a>, I've learned how important some seemingly small but focused foreign policy decisions can be. We must urge Sens. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., and Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., to support the Global Child Thrive Reauthorization Act if we want to keep early childhood development a priority in U.S. foreign assistance. When children are given a stronger start, the cycle of poverty loses its deepest root.</p><p><i>Gabriel Smithdahl, Syracuse University student,</i> <i>Irving Park</i></p><h3>Taxi drivers run circles around the amateurs</h3><p>After reading the recent Sun-Times<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/07/20/amid-changing-industry-chicago-cabbies-and-ride-hailing-drivers-are-both-struggling-im-stuck-in-this" > article on Chicago cabdrivers</a>, I can say I have had more white-knuckle rides in Ubers and Lyfts than I ever had in a taxi. </p><p>I had an Uber driver who sideswiped a car on a side street and just continued driving without any comment about the incident. Another Uber driver seemed terrified of driving on the Eisenhower Expressway and only drove about 40 mph. Luckily, we weren't rear-ended. </p><p>I now only take cabs and have never had a problem. You can tell the difference between a professional driver and the "average citizen" Uber or Lyft driver.</p><p><i>Michael Shawgo, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Medical sharps letter and blunt observations </h3><p>As much as I appreciated Irina Butler’s well-intentioned warnings in her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/07/20/disposing-medical-sharps-local-journalism-nexstar-tegna-russia-ukraine-aragon" >recent letter </a>about medical sharps disposal, my follow-up on her advice created more frustration than assurance.</p><p>A quick search on her listed <a class="Link" href="http://myoldmeds.com/" target="_blank" >myoldmeds.com</a> offered a half dozen disposal sites near me that accepted meds but not sharps.</p><p>Additionally, I wondered if the same sites accepted other such sharps as hobbyists' used razor blades, X-Acto blades, scissors, etc. They are all equally dangerous in the disposal stream as medical sharps.</p><p>A more thorough discussion would have been helpful.</p><p><i>Dennis Allen, Wilmette</i></p><h3>Don’t discount youths’ hope, curiosity </h3><p>I am encouraged, but not shocked by Sean Murphy's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/17/young-poets-anthology-hope-sean-murphy" >recent op-ed</a> on young people and their thoughtful poems. I have been doing Holocaust presentations in mostly middle and high schools for four years now. I consistently leave my talks with the feeling that young people are underrated, smarter than we think and not totally buried in their phones.</p><p>They ask great questions, meaning they listened/heard, and critical thinking is not gone. It is nice to hear their hope is in their heads, hearts and poetry.</p><p><i>Marty Zak, Glenview</i></p><h3>That bully got lucky</h3><p>I’m wondering if the <a class="Link" href="https://www.tmz.com/2026/07/21/chicago-cubs-fan-national-anthem-slap-explanation/" target="_blank" >Cub fan who went viral</a> for slapping a younger man for not standing up for our national anthem would hit a woman or another older man if they did the same.</p><p><i>Chester Pojack, Glendale Heights</i></p>

entries.title: Pete Hegseth should know more testosterone won't make a tougher soldier
entries.summary: <p>How low is too low when it comes to testosterone levels? When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that U.S. service members ages 30 and older will have their <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/hegseth-pentagon-testosterone-testing-troops-47333bbf3af9e4cac432722332ff1383" target="_blank" >testosterone tested every year</a>, neither he nor the Pentagon specified what level of the hormone would be considered “low” enough to require treatment — a telling omission, since <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/16/health/testosterone-explainer-military-testing-wellness" target="_blank" >where “low” begins</a> depends on the lab conducting the test and the guidelines your doctor follows.</p><p>The announcement lands amid a national testosterone craze: Prescriptions have climbed to nearly <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/12/magazine/testosterone-masculinity-trump-rfk.html" target="_blank" >12 million in 2025, up 154% since 2020</a>, and fastest among men in their late 30s and 40s. <a class="Link" href="https://wewillcure.com/insights/therapeutics/care-delivery/startups-disrupt-testosterone-therapy-market-as-younger-men-fuel-demand" target="_blank" >Online clinics</a> that sell testosterone as a lifestyle upgrade have largely driven this rise in prescriptions.</p><p>As a <a class="Link" href="https://psychology.richmond.edu/faculty/astanaland/" target="_blank" >psychologist who studies masculinity</a>, I’m certain that while the idea that more testosterone makes a man tougher and more fit to fight seems intuitive, it’s also mostly wrong.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dc0000" name="module-dc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Testosterone is often <a class="Link" href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/testosterone-in-women" target="_blank" >considered a “male” hormone</a>, but people of every gender produce it in differing amounts.</p><p>In cisgender boys and men, testosterone levels rise at puberty, helping build muscle, grow body hair and produce sperm. Levels naturally decline in adulthood, typically beginning age 30 and onward. When levels drop significantly below normal and a person begins to <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.3949/ccjm.91a.23064" target="_blank" >experience symptoms</a> such as extreme fatigue, low libido or drastic muscle loss, testosterone replacement therapy with medical supervision can help.</p><p>But “normal” is a vast range. Endocrinologists consider testosterone levels between <a class="Link" href="https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/testosterone-deficiency-guideline" target="_blank" >roughly 300 to 1,000 nanograms per deciliter</a> as healthy. Within that range, a man’s testosterone level tells you little about the “masculine” traits that some people think it governs.</p><p>Testosterone is tied to muscle mass, but in healthy men, it <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2025.1512268" target="_blank" >doesn’t track with actual strength</a> — training, sleep and nutrition matter far more. As endocrinologist Adrian Dobs put it, a person at 700 <a class="Link" href="https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/jul/16/hegseth-touts-a-high-testosterone-military-as-doct/" target="_blank" >isn’t stronger or more of a man</a> than one at 300.</p><p>Moreover, an individual’s testosterone levels aren’t fixed — they swing by the hour and the season. So doctors usually test testosterone levels only when symptoms appear. Screening healthy men by the millions may be <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-01408-9" target="_blank" >potentially harmful</a>.</p><p>For instance, testosterone therapy often carries risks. Supplementing the hormone signals the body to shut down production of its own supply, which can <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/sexual-health/in-depth/testosterone-therapy/art-20045728" target="_blank" >shrink the testicles and suppress sperm</a>. Some researchers have even studied testosterone for its <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.5534/wjmh.180036" target="_blank" >contraceptive effects</a>.</p><p>Moreover, because testosterone revs up oil glands and hair follicles — and partly converts them to estrogen — it can also bring about <a class="Link" href="https://www.drugs.com/sfx/testosterone-side-effects.html" target="_blank" >acne, balding</a> and even some <a class="Link" href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/sexual-health/in-depth/testosterone-therapy/art-20045728" target="_blank" >breast tissue</a> growth.</p><p>This “high-T” ideal — sold by online clinics and now endorsed from the top — glosses over these severe risks.</p><h3>The macho myth</h3><p>Decades of research undercut Hegseth’s core claim that more testosterone means a more aggressive, dominant, masculine man.</p><p>A 2001 analysis of data from 45 studies covering nearly 10,000 people found <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1359-1789(00)00032-X" target="_blank" >only a small correlation</a> between testosterone levels and aggression. When researchers pooled data in 2020 from experiments that actually administered testosterone to participants to study whether it causes aggression, they <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yhbeh.2019.104644" target="_blank" >found only weak evidence</a>. In fact, they saw that the effects of testosterone on aggression primarily showed up in men who were more dominant or impulsive.</p><p>If anything, the arrow runs the opposite way — behavior drives testosterone levels. One study found that men who <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01745.x" target="_blank" >handled a gun</a> for 15 minutes had bigger testosterone spikes and acted more aggressively than men who touched a board game. Meanwhile, the testosterone levels of new fathers fell more steeply the more they <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1105403108" target="_blank" >physically cared for their child</a>.</p><p>When men do demonstrate aggression, the trigger is typically social. In my own research, <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167220984298" target="_blank" >threatening a man’s sense of manhood</a> — but not a woman’s womanhood — reliably provokes aggression, and the men who react most strongly are those who feel the most pressure to live up to masculine ideals.</p><p>The link between aggression and the fear of failing at manhood takes root early. In a study of more than 200 adolescent boys and their parents, my team and I found that boys who reacted aggressively to threats to their masculinity were mainly those who felt <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/gender-conformity-starts-young-and-boys-and-girls-fall-in-line-in-different-ways-275996" target="_blank" >external pressure to be masculine</a>. That pressure was strongest among boys whose parents endorsed specific beliefs about manhood, like the idea that men should hold power over others.</p><p>Biology, social pressure and development work together to determine how a boy grows into a man. Unlike Hegseth’s story that manhood is a chemical to be topped off, research shows that while hormones may open a window, the social environment decides what comes through.</p><h3>Military life lowers testosterone</h3><p>Ironically, the grind of military service can drive down a man’s testosterone levels.</p><p>A 2020 study of U.S. Army Rangers found that the <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.23937/2469-5718/1510169" target="_blank" >sleep loss built into training</a> significantly reduced testosterone levels.</p><p>Chronic stress, sleep deprivation, blast exposure and poor nutrition can produce a cluster of health problems called “<a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0091217420906659" target="_blank" >Operator Syndrome</a>.” In some cases, the <a class="Link" href="https://taskandpurpose.com/military-life/low-testosterone-operator-syndrome-sof/" target="_blank" >work conditions of special operators</a> can push a 35-year-old’s testosterone levels toward those typical of a man in his 80s.</p><p>Notice the loop: The military imposes the very conditions that suppress testosterone, then proposes to fix the result with more of it. The psychologist who named Operator Syndrome cautioned that handing troops testosterone <a class="Link" href="https://taskandpurpose.com/news/pentagon-testosterone-treatment/" target="_blank" >won’t restore their health</a>, because the real culprits are sleep, stress and injury.</p><p>In February 2025, the Pentagon <a class="Link" href="https://www.military.com/daily-news/2025/02/10/transgender-recruits-and-gender-affirming-health-care-restricted-hegseth-memo.html" target="_blank" >halted gender-affirming hormone therapy</a> for transgender troops, framing such care as incompatible with the force’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/02/03/2025-02178/prioritizing-military-excellence-and-readiness" target="_blank" >“readiness” and “lethality.”</a> Yet prescribing testosterone to bring a cisgender man’s body in line with the Pentagon’s masculine ideals is hormone therapy, too.</p><p>Legal advocates <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/high-t-department-war-hegseth-210357191.html" target="_blank" >flagged the contradiction</a> at once: The same class of medication is disqualifying for one group of service members, but for another, it’s rebranded as optimizing the soldier.</p><p>So a testosterone mandate won’t build tougher soldiers — if anything, it reveals an anxiety no hormone can fix. My research argues that the men most pressured to prove their manhood are the ones who <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10888683221141176" target="_blank" >most experience it as fragile</a>, treating masculinity as a status that can be lost and must be won back again and again.</p><p>Telling troops that their readiness hinges on a test result can <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1037/men0000468" target="_blank" >deepen their anxiety around manhood</a>. Real strength — the kind that holds up under fire — is not something that can be topped off with a hormone. Although testosterone is biologically useful, it isn’t the measure of a man or soldier.</p><p><i>Adam Stanaland, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Richmond.</i></p><p><i>A version of this </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/more-testosterone-wont-make-a-better-soldier-or-a-tougher-man-aggression-and-strength-drive-t-levels-not-the-other-way-around-287828" target="_blank" ><i>article</i></a><i> first appeared on </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/us" target="_blank" ><i>The Conversation</i></a><i>, a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scholars.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-f80000" name="html-embed-module-f80000"></a><iframe src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287828/count.gif?distributor=republish-lightbox-advanced" width="1" height="1" style="border: none !important" referrerpolicy="no-referrer-when-downgrade"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-960000" name="module-960000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Laos' famous beer brand Beerlao makes a splash in the Midwest
entries.summary: <p>Stacy Seuamsothabandith, CEO of Laos to Your House, fondly remembers her Lao relatives drinking Beerlao at family gatherings during her childhood in the Quad Cities.</p><p>Beerlao, brewed with Lao jasmine rice and European malt, hops and yeast, is considered the national beer of Laos. It was hard to find in the Chicago area until Laos to Your House recently became Beerlao’s importer in some Midwest states. The food business imports the beer directly from Lao Brewing Co. in Laos. Its first shipment arrived in Illinois in June.</p><p>The rice in Beerlao gives it a smooth finish that goes well with southeast Asian cuisine, Byron Gully, chief operating officer of Laos to Your House, said. Many customers asked the founders to bring Beerlao to Illinois.</p><p>Because of Laos to Your House, Beerlao is now sold more widely in big stores such as select Garfield Beverage Warehouse locations and Sam’s Club in Rockford and Elgin. Starting in September, Sam’s Club will sell the beer in Montgomery, about 40 miles southwest of Chicago, and two locations near Minneapolis in Eagan and White Bear Lake. </p><p>Beerlao has importers on the east and west coasts, but its previous Midwest distributor stopped selling it years ago. But last year, Laos to Your House got limited distribution for Illinois, followed by rights to distribute to big retailers in Illinois, Minnesota, Iowa and Wisconsin. </p><p>Beerlao is also carried by Vietnamese restaurant Saigon Sisters in the West Loop.</p><p>It goes “very well with our food and I want to introduce it to my diners because it’s so hard to find,” Saigon Sisters owner Mary Nguyen Aregoni said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1f0000" name="image-1f0000"></a> Beerlao has sentimental value for her.</p><p>“I want to carry great Asian beers, and I had Beerlao during my travels in Laos with my mom. And it was a backpackers favorite and hard to find in the U.S.,” she said.</p><p>And it tastes good. “It's like Belgian style and more complex than standard lager beer,” Aregoni said. “It’s not Bud Light.”</p><p>An 8-ounce bottle costs $6.50 at Saigon Sisters.</p><p>Demand for Beerlao has been strong and Laos to Your House hopes to bring the beer to more big retailers.<b> </b>It expects its next shipment — a container of Beerlao with more than 28,000 bottles — to arrive in the U.S. in September.</p><p>Laos to Your House is a family-owned food business based at The Hatchery Chicago, an incubator in East Garfield Park. Its ready-made Lao dishes are in 12 Mariano’s in the Chicago area, as well as select Foxtrot and Fresh Market stores.</p><p>Beer fits with the company’s goal to ensure that Laos is no longer the “forgotten” Asian country.</p><p>“Every bottle of Beerlao represents an opportunity not only for someone to enjoy a great beer, but also to start a conversation about Laos,” Seuamsothabandith said. “If someone picks up a bottle because they're curious and then learns something about the country, its people or its cuisine, we've accomplished something far greater than simply making a sale. That's exactly what our mission is about.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f00000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Beerlao is brewed with Lao jasmine rice and European malt, hops and yeast.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Laos to Your House launched in 2022, with Seuamsothabandith as CEO and her brother Keo Seuam as executive chef. Their parents were refugees from Laos who immigrated to the U.S. in the late 1970s, due to war in southeast Asia. Gully, Seuamsothabandith’s husband, joined full-time in 2024.</p><p>Fluctuating tariffs last year were a challenge but settled at about 10% for products from Laos. But that could change any time, Gully said. The current tariff will expire near the end of July. It’s unclear what will happen next.</p><p>“This is one of the many things that make it so hard for a small business to take a chance: the uncertainty in the administration’s policies,” Gully said.</p><p>“Our supply chain will be longer now and more risky, especially since we are importing directly from Laos. Anything that impacts shipping — wars, the cost of fuel — will impact us,” he said.</p><p>But that doesn’t deter consumers. Beerlao is in Sam’s Club because its customers in Rockford, home to a sizable southeast Asian community, asked the retailer to stock the beer. Sam’s Club started looking for someone to supply it and came across Laos to Your House, which was just starting to import Beerlao.</p><p>“It was really the Lao movement that bubbled Beerlao up to the surface. Then through searching, Sam’s Club found us and reached out,” Seuamsothabandith said.</p><p>“Beerlao is a great example of how listening to our members helps us deliver authentic finds,” Madelyn Yates, merchant at Sam’s Club, said in a statement.</p><p>“Who would have thought Beerlao would be in a big box retailer next to Heineken?” Seuamsothabandith said.</p><p>It’s another step in Laos to Your House’s mission to elevate Laos, first through food and now through beer.</p>

entries.title: Besides Obama, Chicago produced a second president and he's about to turn 100
entries.summary: <p>VILNIUS, Lithuania — Valdas Adamkus is one of the most beloved political figures in his country, serving as Lithuania's president for two separate five-year terms in a transformative period just before and after it joined the European Union and NATO.</p><p>He's turning 100 in the fall, and commemorations are already being planned around the country. But on an April morning inside the living room of his stately home on the outskirts of Vilnius, he asks, "How is the Deep Tunnel?"</p><p>The question about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" >Chicago’s Tunnel and Reservoir Plan</a> — created to protect Lake Michigan and contain the city's flood water — is logical. Adamkus spent nearly half his life in Chicago and ran the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Region 5 office from 1981 to 1997. </p><p>He commuted to Chicago from Hinsdale with a mission to keep the Great Lakes clean, including keeping raw sewage out of Lake Michigan. Even now, some Lithuanian Americans — among an estimated 60,000 in Chicago — like to boast that Adamkus cleaned up the lake.</p><p>When he first ran for president in 1998, his critics said he wasn't Lithuanian enough. </p><p>But he was the man for the moment: An Americanized Lithuanian who led the country toward the European Union and NATO, in the decade after its 1990 independence. Lithuania joined the EU and NATO in spring 2004, following Adamkus' first five-year term.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former President of Lithuania Valdas Adamkus, 99, sits for an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times in his home outside Vilnius on April 14.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>He was born Valdemaras Adamkavičius — a name he would later legally shorten — on Nov. 3, 1926 in Kaunas.</p><p>As a teenager, he joined the Lithuanian resistance during World War II, then fled with his parents to Germany, when the Soviets solidified their occupation of Lithuania in 1944.</p><p>He immigrated to the U.S. in 1949, getting a job in Chicago in a car parts factory. He went on to work as a draftsman for an engineering firm, and in 1961, he earned a civil engineering degree from the Illinois Institute of Technology in Bronzeville.</p><p>Though he was firmly in Chicago and a naturalized U.S. citizen, he stayed tied to his homeland and was active in several diaspora organizations.</p><p>He married Alma Nutautaitė, his sweetheart from when they were refugees in Germany, and they settled in a Lithuanian enclave in Marquette Park, later moving to Hinsdale.</p><p>Adamkus joined the EPA in 1970 and was named regional director in 1981 by then-President Ronald Reagan, overseeing Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio and Wisconsin until 1997. He used his government position to travel to Lithuania and push for Lithuanian independence whenever he could.</p><p>"It was always on our mind," he says. "I had the opportunity, personally, to approach the highest levels of the government, and my contact with the congressional delegation definitely was very close."</p><p>In meetings with U.S. presidents, "we talked not only about the environment. I had the opportunity to explain when the president asked, 'How is Lithuania doing?' And that was the opportunity, really, to discuss the issues," he says.</p><p>When he first visited Lithuania in 1972 after more than a quarter-century abroad, Adamkus says he was stunned by the effects of Soviet repression on the Lithuanians he met.</p><p>"Instead of meeting in a normal situation, when you can discuss the issues, the culture, the funders, I found a community which did not speak, did not communicate," he says. "People were walking, looking at the sidewalk. run in Lithuania's 1998 presidential election, he cited wanting to rid the country of corruption and old Soviet ways and gain closer ties to the West. He told The Associated Press at the time that "a generation grew up in a strict one-party state, was told what to do and what not to do. I am bringing experience of openness and individual initiative, which is unknown in this society for 50 years."</p><p>But he had to overcome two obstacles.</p><p>The first was getting a court's approval to run for president, as there was a residency requirement. Even though he'd obtained his Lithuanian citizenship again in 1992, he had lived in the U.S. for most of his life.</p><p>The second hurdle was convincing Alma to move.</p><p>"She was very, very strongly against that idea," he says.</p><p>His wife, who died at 95 in 2023, wanted a quiet retirement filled with travel and hobbies. But supporters in Lithuania were pressing him to run, and he says he became convinced that he should try.</p><p>"I have to admit that a lot of tears were shared about my decision," he says. "But finally I can say that Alma was such a good soldier."</p><p>He ran as an independent and won by a margin of about 14,000 votes. Adamkus credited diaspora voters in the Chicago area with helping him eke out his first victory.</p><p>He lost reelection in 2003 to Rolandas Paksas, who was later impeached and removed after a corruption scandal involving a Russian businessman and campaign funder.</p><p>Adamkus was reelected in June 2004, serving until 2009.</p><p>"He's photogenic. He's able to speak in several languages. He knows how to work both the small talk and the high-level talk," says Arūnas Pemkus, who grew up in the Chicago area and worked for the U.S. Department of State in the late '80s and early '90s. As a politician, "he was a fish in water."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5b0000" ambassador and current parliamentarian Žygimantas Pavilionis says Adamkus, like other diaspora people of his time, "was the incarnation of something that was preserved and saved in America."</p><p>"We still love him the most, I would say, because of his American spirit — because it is also the old Lithuanian spirit, the spirit that [the diaspora] saved in Chicago," Pavilionis says.</p><p>Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., says Adamkus' example lives on in Lithuania's support for Ukraine and for democratic activists forced to flee Russia and Belarus.</p><p>"President Valdas Adamkus has committed his life to the Lithuanian people and the fight for democracy," Durbin says. "My mother, a Lithuanian immigrant, would be proud of her birth country — thanks to my friend, President Adamkus."</p><p>When asked how he sees his own legacy, Adamkus paused, saying it's a difficult question.</p><p>"I believe there is no need to wish how to be remembered," he says. "You should feel if you really have contributed with your life. And I personally believe that when I ask myself, have I done what I wanted? entries.title: Man shot and killed in West Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot while sitting in his vehicle early Saturday in West Garfield Park. </p><p>The man, 37, was inside his vehicle in the 4200 block of West Monroe Street when a male suspect approached him and fired shots around 2:13 a.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>He suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his body and was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His name hasn't been released. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 2 shot, including 5-year-old boy, in Little Italy
entries.summary: <p>A 5-year-old boy and a man were hurt in a drive-by shooting early Saturday in Little Italy on the Near West Side. </p><p>A group was gathered in the 1000 block of West 14th Street around 12:35 a.m. when a vehicle pulled up and someone from inside opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>The boy was shot in the abdomen and was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition, police said. A 39-year-old man was struck in the buttocks and was taken to the same hospital in good condition. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Review: Benson Boone is a ‘Wanted Man’ — but who is he really?
entries.summary: <p>It took approximately 13-and-a-half-minutes for a backflip on Friday night. It’s hard to know if that’s a Benson Boone record of some kind, or whether the number of backflips he subsequently pulled off — about five or six for those keeping count — was sufficient. In some cities, there’s reportedly been as many as 10.</p><p>The fact that there even are flip counters and fans debating if his soft rolls into the crowd count (maybe it’s a .5?) is quite wild. It can’t just be a regular concert anymore — it has to be the Olympics, too? Still, the acrobatic feat is a huge part of what makes Boone a “Wanted Man” — and he’s not going to let anyone down.</p><p>As the 24-year-old tumbled into a packed Allstate Arena on his latest tour, he was clearly committed to giving the people what they wanted. Wearing a vest that bared his chest to show off his hot-guy calendar abs. Donning a backpack as a wink to fans who have turned the accessory into some kind of Boone lore on social media. Easily unleashing his unbelievable vocal range and perfect-pitch falsetto. Attacking the piano with great balls of fire energy on “Mr Electric Blue.” Saving his YouTube Billion Views Club hit “Beautiful Things” for the end so it lingers. And packing in a boatload of ’70s and ’80s Easter eggs with a “Star Wars”-themed intro, mustachioed Freddie Mercury cosplay and songs like “Young American Heart” that sounded an awful lot like “We Didn’t Start the Fire” while paired with video graphics of embers burning in the background.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Benson Boone performs in Baltimore, Maryland, as part of his Wanted Man Tour. The singer performed at Allstate Arena in Rosemont on Friday, the first of a two-night stand in the Chicago area.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Shayden Schoonover</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kids loved it. Dads loved it. Moms <i>really</i> loved it. Like the musical equivalent of a Pixar movie made for a young audience with all the adult side jabs, Boone has successfully carved out his multi-generational stake. But it all felt a little too … much. For no clear reason. It's a danger of being a people pleaser — it often leads to a false sense of connection.</p><p>“My greatest fear is to show up to this stage, to write songs, to do all of this for no one and to have no one at the end of the day. That’s what I’m the most scared of,” Boone interestingly admitted as he introduced the song “My Greatest Fear” midway through the night. While that’s nothing he has to worry about anytime soon — he just logged his 10th Billboard<i> </i>Hot 100 hit with “The Time of My Life” — there is always the question of longevity with an artist like Boone. One that found virality early and then was explicitly marketed for mass appeal rather than taking the time to find his niche. There’s no doubt the talent is there, but not so much the strategy.</p><p>The Wanted Man Tour’s biggest crime is having too many aliases to know Boone’s true identity. The first few songs — “Sorry I’m Here for Someone Else,” “Mr Electric Blue,” “There She Goes” and “Wanted Man” — were an incredible show of force with a magnetic four-piece band (whom he sadly never introduced) that sent shockwaves of arena rock. Yet the next hour was dragged down by a nearly 12-song extended pop ballad that grew stale beyond a few high points.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" In his Friday night show, he performed about five or six for those keeping count.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Shayden Schoonover</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That included his Technicolor ’80s pop gem “Mystical Magical,” which erupted into a mass singalong. Another highlight was his unreleased song “Traveler,” a dynamo track performed solo at a stripped-down B stage. Written with incredible emotion, it moves away from copy-and-paste heartbreak hymns into something spectacular. If his team is smart, it’ll be his next single. The other standout was the family tribute “Momma Song” that was accompanied by home video, with one segment even capturing Boone’s first baby flip.</p><p>Like any well-rounded artist, Boone has many sides to him, but they often feel like fragmented parts rather than adding up to one cohesive whole. He’s been dragged in a million different directions since breaking out. Ten years ago, the Mormon teen from Washington was a competitive diver and tennis player before literally finding his voice in a battle of the bands competition. Soon after, he found some viral moments on TikTok and auditioned for “American Idol” in 2021. The judges loved him, but he stepped away from the competition to make it on his own. Imagine Dragons’ Dan Reynolds stepped up to sign him to his imprint and Boone has been coasting on “Beautiful Things” and backflips ever since.</p><p>Yes, all of it may make him a “Wanted Man,” but at some point you hope he stops caring about that and really finds who he wants to be too.</p><p><b></b></p><h3>Benson Boone set list for July 24, 2026 show at Allstate Arena</h3><p>Sorry I'm Here for Someone Else<br>Mr Electric Blue<br>There She Goes<br>Wanted Man<br>Drunk in My Mind<br>Slow It Down<br>Mystical Magical<br>Pretty Slowly<br>In the Stars<br>My Greatest Fear<br>Take Me Home<br>Young American Heart<br>Traveler<br>Momma Song<br>Before You<br>The Time of My Life<br>I Wanna Be the One You Call<br>What Was<br>Cry<br>Beautiful Things</p>
